items.q: What happens when start() is called a second time on the same Thread object?
options: It runs the target again in a new thread
It raises RuntimeError: threads can only be started once
It is ignored without a message
rationales: It does not start another run; a Thread object can be started once.
There is no silent form; the second call raises an error.

options: The thread prints Cats Dogs
print runs at once in the main thread and the thread is given None as its target
Python raises TypeError at the Thread call
rationales: The call print(...) has already run, in the main thread, before Thread was created.
Thread accepts target=None, so no error is raised; the thread then does nothing.

items.q: join(0.1) is called on a thread that needs 0.6 s. How do you tell that the timeout happened?
options: join() returns False
The thread's is_alive() is still True
join() raises TimeoutError
rationales: join(timeout) always returns None, whatever happened.
No exception is raised; the caller must test is_alive().

items.q: The main thread ends while a daemon thread is still sleeping before a print. What happens to it?
options: The program waits for it and the print happens
It is stopped abruptly at shutdown and never prints
It becomes a normal thread
rationales: Only non-daemon threads keep the program alive.
A daemon flag does not change when the thread is stopped at shutdown.

items.q: Why can two threads that both run counter += 1 on a shared counter lose an update?
options: The statement compiles to several bytecode steps (read, add, store) and a switch can fall between them
Python forbids two threads from reading one variable
The second thread always gets a copy of the counter
rationales: Threads may read the same variable; the problem is the steps between read and store.
They share the variable, not a copy; that is the reason the update is lost.

items.q: A thread holds a plain threading.Lock and asks for the same lock again with a timeout of 0.2 s. What does acquire return, and what would an RLock give?
options: False for the Lock and True for the RLock
True for both
False for both
rationales: A Lock is not reentrant: the second request waits and times out, while an RLock lets its owner in.
An RLock lets the thread that holds it acquire it again.

items.q: Two threads each take two locks, one in the order A then B and the other B then A, with a pause between the two takes. After join(1.0) both are still alive. What is this?
options: A deadlock: each waits for the lock the other holds
A lost update
A daemon thread that was stopped
rationales: Nothing was lost: both threads are blocked, not computing.
Neither thread is a daemon; they are waiting for each other.

items.q: ThreadPoolExecutor.map runs three tasks that finish in reverse order. In what order are its results?
options: The order of the inputs: [0, 1, 2]
The order in which the tasks finished: [2, 1, 0]
An arbitrary order
rationales: That is the order of as_completed, not of map.
map returns the results in the order of the inputs.

items.q: A task submitted to a pool raises ValueError('boom'). When does the main program notice?
options: At once, as a traceback in the main thread
Only when result() is called on its Future, which raises it again
Never; pool tasks cannot raise
rationales: The exception stays in the Future and is silent until it is asked for.
It is stored: result() raises it and exception() returns it.

items.q: A pool has one worker and five queued 0.2 s tasks. The first has started. How many tasks does shutdown(cancel_futures=True) cancel?
options: 4: the ones that had not started
5: all of them
0: a pool cannot cancel tasks
rationales: A task that has started cannot be cancelled, so the first one finishes.
cancel_futures=True cancels the pending futures, which here are four.

items.q: Four CPU-bound tasks take 0.89 s one after another on the standard Python 3.14.6 build. About how long do they take on 4 threads?
options: About 0.2 s, a quarter of the time
About 1.0 s, no faster than one after another
About 3.5 s, four times slower
rationales: That would need four cores running Python code at once, which the global interpreter lock does not allow.
The recorded run took 1.003 s: no speed-up and a little overhead.

items.q: Eight sleeps of 0.5 s took 4.001 s one after another. Why do 8 threads take about 0.5 s?
options: The lock is released while a thread waits, so the waits overlap
Each thread sleeps for one eighth of the time
The sleeps are skipped when threads are used
rationales: Each thread still waits the full 0.5 s; the waits happen together.
Nothing is skipped; the waits overlap.

items.q: Which setting turns the global interpreter lock on again for the free-threaded build?
options: PYTHON_GIL=1 (or the option -X gil=1)
PYTHON_GIL=0
sys.setswitchinterval(0.0001)
rationales: PYTHON_GIL=0 leaves it off.
The switch interval only changes how often threads that hold the lock may switch.

items.q: The study did not run the free-threaded build of Python 3.13. What may this page say about it?
options: Only what the documentation says, marked NOT EXECUTED
That it behaves like the free-threaded 3.14.6 build
Nothing; it is never mentioned
rationales: The 3.14.6 result must not be carried over to a build that was not run.
The study names what it did not run, so that a reader does not mistake documentation for a result.
